title: What are blue laws?
summary: Josh and Chuck explain blue laws: restrictions on activities, especially on Sundays, rooted in Christian Sabbath observance. They trace origins from the Ten Commandments and the shift of the Sabbath to Sunday, through early Christian councils and Roman emperors, colonial laws (including Jamestown's harsh 1610 code), and the disestablishment debate that led to Sabbatarians vs. anti-Sabbatarians fights and compromise exceptions. They cover surviving examples (Georgia alcohol sales, New York brunch hours, car dealership bans in Texas, Illinois and North Dakota, Maine hunting, Bergen County NJ shopping, North Dakota exceptions, Maryland tobacco), the legality through McGowan v. Maryland (1961) where the Supreme Court upheld blue laws, Lyman Stone's secular argument for them, studies on alcohol consumption, church attendance, and retail, and theories on why they're called blue laws. The episode closes with a listener mail about the thought-terminating cliche "I don't know about that."

segments.title: Opening banter and episode preview
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce blue laws as Chuck's pick, define them as old laws restricting activities on certain days (especially Sundays), mention Georgia's former Sunday alcohol ban, and preview the structure: history, wacky laws, then legality.

segments.title: Origins of the Sabbath moving to Sunday
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the Ten Commandments' Sabbath commandment, the Jewish Saturday Sabbath, and early Christianity's move to Sunday between the second and fifth centuries, which overlapped with pagan Sun worship. They mention possible early laws, including the Council of Laodicea around 363 AD and Roman emperors such as Constantine in 321.

segments.title: Protestants, Puritans, and colonial Sunday laws
segments.summary: Christian rulers issued Sabbath rules for centuries. Martin Luther reportedly was less strict about Sunday specifically, while Protestants and Puritans later became strong enforcers of Sunday blue laws in America. A story says George Washington was stopped by a sheriff for traveling to church on a Sunday, since travel and harnessing horses counted as labor.

segments.title: Jamestown's harsh blue laws
segments.summary: Jamestown enacted blue laws in 1610, requiring church attendance and banning other Sunday activity. Punishments escalated: first offense meant a week without food, second meant losing allowance and whipping, and third meant death.

segments.title: Disestablishment and the anti-disestablishmentarian backlash
segments.summary: The hosts explain disestablishment, the separation of government from supporting particular churches, influenced by Thomas Jefferson and the English context. They describe the later backlash by evangelical Protestants, who tried to use politics to keep America Protestant, a movement they call anti-disestablishmentarianism.

segments.title: Industry vs. Sabbatarians and the compromise
segments.summary: Growing business during the Second Industrial Revolution clashed with the Sabbath-day rest. Strange alliances formed: labor unions, Jewish people, Seventh-day Adventists, and secular people often opposed Sabbatarians. The Sabbatarians were louder and better organized, and the result was a long compromise with carved-out exceptions.

segments.title: Exceptions and surviving blue laws
segments.summary: Exceptions grew over time, such as beach ice cream sales while town storekeepers could not sell it. The hosts discuss surviving laws: Georgia's Sunday alcohol sales until noon, New York brunch rules, Texas, Illinois and North Dakota car sales bans, the Texas Jewish and Seventh-day Adventist dealer exception, and the NFL's Saturday game restrictions.

segments.title: Other state and county examples
segments.summary: Maine and Virginia restrict hunting on Sundays; Maine formerly banned department store shopping until 1990s. Bergen County, New Jersey bans most shopping on Sundays, helping mom-and-pop stores against big box competition, and has resisted repeal. North Dakota's exceptions list includes ice cream, newspapers, cigars, and medicine. Texas once allowed blank videotapes but not recorded ones. Maryland exempted tobacco.

segments.title: Legality: McGowan v. Maryland and the Supreme Court
segments.summary: Blue laws are mostly state and local, not federal. The Supreme Court in McGowan v. Maryland (1961) upheld them 8-1; Chief Justice Earl Warren argued they serve secular well-being, and Justice William O. Douglas dissented, saying they effectively support Christian Sunday observance. The hosts discuss Lyman Stone's argument that blue laws are a progressive way to give workers a shared day off, and the paradox of closing businesses people want on Sunday.

segments.title: Studies on blue laws and origin of the name
segments.summary: Studies find repealing blue laws does not increase car accidents from Sunday drinking; a Georgia county comparison showed little difference in alcohol consumption; retail spending stayed similar; an MIT 2008 study found repeal lowered church attendance and donations and raised drinking and drug use. The name origin is uncertain; the Puritan blue paper theory is unverified, and slang like blue nose and blue stocking may be related.

segments.title: Listener mail and sign-off
segments.summary: Listener Rebecca writes about the thought-terminating cliche 'I don't know about that,' and the hosts sign off with a plug for the show.
